en: The Treatise on the Realization of the Self composed by Ācārya Śaṅkara (with commentary).

This realization of the Self is intended for those whose sins have been exhausted through austerities, who are tranquil, free from passion, and seekers of liberation; it is prescribed as that which must be sought by such persons.
*Ātmabodha-Ṭīkā*:
*Oṃ*, salutations to Durgā.

Therein, the venerable Śaṅkarācārya, having composed the three systems of Vedānta for those of superior qualification, now desires to present the treatise titled *Ātmabodha*, a compendium of the established conclusions of Vedānta, for the benefit of those of dull intellect who are unable to study those [three systems]. He makes this formal declaration with the words: "By austerities... (*tapobhiḥ*).

The meaning is that this realization of the Self is enjoined—that is, it is presented as a necessary duty by way of a positive injunction—for those who have diminished their sins and internal defects such as attachment through austerities consisting of the constant and occasional performance of *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa* penances; for those who are thus "peaceful," meaning whose mental dispositions are undisturbed; for those "free from passion," meaning devoid of the desire to enjoy fruits in this world or the next; and for those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*), who have exerted themselves in breaking the knots of worldly existence and are endowed with the aforementioned means. This is because of the scriptural statement: "By the constant and occasional [rites] alone, one effects the destruction of evil. 1.
For awakening is the direct and sole means to liberation among all other means;

without knowledge, liberation is not accomplished, just as cooking is not accomplished without fire. [2] Now, since there exist many means such as austerity, yoga, mantras, ritual action, and sacrifice, why is awakening alone stated to be the primary one with respect to liberation? To this he says: "Awakening is [the sole means] among others..."

Austerities, yoga, mantra, ritual action, sacrifice, and other such means accomplish liberation through knowledge by way of a traditional succession; however, knowledge alone, by its very arising, destroys ignorance entirely and consecrates the seeker of liberation in self-sovereignty (*svārājya*). Therefore, the primacy of knowledge over other means has been stated.
He confirms this very point with an illustration: "Of cooking" (*pākasya*).

Just as in the world, although the acts of cooking and the means such as wood, water, and vessels exist, [the meal] is not accomplished without fire, so too liberation is not accomplished without knowledge—this is the meaning.
Action does not remove ignorance because it is not its opposite;
knowledge alone destroys ignorance, just as light destroys a mass of darkness.

Now, one might object: "Since actions possess diverse potencies, action itself will destroy ignorance; what is the use of the knowledge of the Self? Anticipating this, he says: "Because it is not opposed [to action]," the meaning of which is clear.
(Verse 3) Due to ignorance, the Self appears as if limited; when that [ignorance] is destroyed, [the Self remains] alone.

For the Self shines by itself, like the sun when the clouds have vanished. (4) Now, one might ask: "Since the Self is perceived as if limited in every body, how can there be liberation (*kaivalya*)? To this he says, "limited" (*paricchinna*). The limitation of the perfect, non-dual Self is merely caused by the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of various high and low bodies imagined through ignorance; it does not exist from the perspective of reality (*tattvadṛṣṭi*). Therefore, through discrimination (*viveka*), upon the removal of non-discrimination, the Self shines forth in its absolute isolation (*kevala*), just as the sun does when the veil of clouds is gone—this is the meaning.

Having rendered the soul, which is turbid with ignorance, stainless through the practice of knowledge, that knowledge itself vanishes of its own accord, like the silt of the *kataka* nut in water. //5//

Now, one might object that the establishment of non-duality through the knowledge of the Self is untenable, because duality is established by cognitive states (vṛtti-jñāna); to this, he says: "It is turbid with ignorance."

The individual soul (*jīva*), which has been defiled by egoism (*ahaṃkāra*) and other factors that are effects of ignorance (*ajñāna*), and which identifies with agency, enjoyership, and so forth—knowledge, through the removal of ignorance by long-term practice, completely destroys its effects such as the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and then itself perishes, because it is an effect of ignorance. Since the mental modification (*vṛtti*) is reflected therein, that knowledge merges into the Self alone, being the appearance of the Self. At that time, the non-dual Self alone shines forth; the meaning is that it is just as when the clearing-nut (*katakareṇu*) makes all water pure and then itself dissolves away.

"Samsara is indeed like a dream, crowded with passion, hatred, and the like; it appears as real during its own time, but upon awakening, it becomes non-existent. (6) Anticipating the objection—"How can samsara, which is experienced through direct perception (*aparokṣatayā*), be absolutely non-existent? This contradicts perception"—the author establishes its falsity by means of the analogy of a dream, stating: "Samsara... and so forth.

Saṃsāra, being crowded with passion, hatred, and the like, appears as if real even though it is illusory, as long as its own cause—ignorance—remains present in its own time. However, upon awakening, when the knowledge of the Self arises from hearing the meaning of the Great Saying (mahāvākya), it becomes non-existent. Here the illustration is "like a dream":

even a dream, while one is experiencing sleep, appears as if true even though it is illusory; yet upon awakening, when sleep is destroyed, the dream becomes false. The meaning is that saṃsāra is exactly like that.
The world appears as real only so long as Brahman— the non-dual substratum of all— is not known, just like the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell.
He confirms the falsity of the world by means of an illustration: "Tāvat" (so long).

Just as the cognition of silver is experienced as if real so long as the specific knowledge of the blue back, the triangular shape, and so forth [of the mother-of-pearl] has not arisen; likewise, so long as Brahman—the non-dual Being-Consciousness-Bliss which is the substratum of all—is not known, that is, not directly experienced, the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) transformed into the form of the world is seen through delusion as if it were real. This is the meaning.

In the Supreme Lord, the substratum of all, who is the self of existence, consciousness, and bliss, and who is eternally pervasive, the worlds proceed through creation, maintenance, and dissolution, like bubbles in water. [8] They are merely conceptualized within Viṣṇu.
All various individual manifestations are like bracelets and other ornaments in gold.

He establishes that the entire visible world of phenomenal expansion (*prapañca*) is imagined through *māyā* in Brahman alone: "In the Being-Consciousness-Self"—that is, in Brahman, which is the Self of Truth, Knowledge, and Bliss, eternal, all-pervasive, and the underlying thread of everything—in that Supreme Lord who is the material cause of all, all individual manifestations—including gods, animals, humans, and both mobile and immobile beings—though diverse, are merely imagined, just as bracelets, crowns, and so forth are [imagined] in gold; the meaning is that they are non-different from Brahman.
Just as the all-pervading Hṛṣīkeśa, like space, appears as if divided due to various limiting adjuncts, yet becomes solitary when those [adjuncts] are destroyed. ||10||
He confirms the stated meaning by means of the analogy of space: "Just as space...

Hṛṣīkeśa—the controller or director of all the senses beginning with the mind—is the omnipresent Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*). Being reflected in the various adjuncts (*upādhi*) fashioned by His own *māyā*, He appears as if manifold; yet when those adjuncts fashioned by *māyā* are destroyed through the knowledge of the oneness of Brahman and the Self, He shines forth as the Absolute alone. Just as space appears as if manifold due to the influence of adjuncts but shines as one alone upon the dissolution of those adjuncts, so it is in this case—this is the meaning.

It is solely due to the influence of various limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) that caste, name, stage of life (*āśrama*), and so forth are superimposed upon the Self, just as distinctions such as taste and color are superimposed upon water. [Objection:
But how can the eternity of the Self be asserted when it is permeated by the respective castes and other attributes in all bodies? To this, he says: "Due to various limiting adjuncts... (verse 11).

It means that caste, name, stage of life (*āśrama*), and so forth are superimposed upon the Self due solely to the influence of various previously mentioned limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*); they are fashioned by *māyā* and do not exist inherently. This is just as water, which is sweet by its own nature, assumes the qualities of pungent, astringent, sour, red, yellow, and other substances when mixed with them, yet it does not possess those qualities by its own essential nature (*svarūpa*).
[The body] is produced from the fivefold-combined (*pañcīkṛta*) great elements and is accumulated through karma.
The body is said to be the locus for the experience of pleasure and pain.
(12) He describes the three limiting adjuncts (upādhi) imagined through the ignorance (avidyā) of the Self: "consisting of the fivefold [elements]," etc.

The process of quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa*) consists of dividing each of the five elements into two equal parts, then subdividing one half of each into four equal portions, and finally joining those portions with the other elements. From these thus quintuplicated gross elements—earth and the other great elements—there arises the gross body, which is accumulated through past actions (*karma*), built up by the accumulation of *prārabdha* karma, and serves as the locus and the site of experience for the inner self (*pratyagātman*) in its enjoyment of pleasure and pain.
This [body] is endowed with the five vital breaths (*prāṇa*), the mind (*manas*), the intellect (*buddhi*), and the ten sense organs.

The subtle body (*sūkṣma-aṅga*), which is the means for experience, arises from the unquintuplicated subtle elements. He describes the subtle limiting adjunct (*sūkṣma-upādhi*): "consisting of the five vital breaths," etc.

The five vital breaths are the functions (*vṛtti*)—namely *prāṇa* and so forth—of the single Great Vital Breath (*mahā-prāṇa*). There are ten sense organs through the distinction of the organs of knowledge (*jñānendriya*) and the organs of action (*karmendriya*). By the word "mind" (*manas*), there is the intellect (*buddhi*), which consists of the function of the internal organ characterized by determination and is composed of volition and doubt. Joined with these, the subtle body—the *liṅga-śarīra*—arises from the subtle elements that have not been quintuplicated; it is born from the subtle elements and is the means for the experience of pleasure and pain. This is the meaning.
The indefinable beginningless ignorance is called the causal limiting adjunct (*kāraṇopādhi*);
one should discern the Self as distinct from these three types of adjuncts.
He states the third limiting adjunct (*upādhi*): "beginningless ignorance" (*anādyavidyā*).

That which is beginningless, indescribable as being or non-being, and the cause of delusion is called the causal adjunct. And because it exists in the form of both individual and collective aggregates (*vyaṣṭi-samaṣṭi*), serving as the cause for the gross and subtle worlds, it is called the causal adjunct.
He states the purpose of mentioning these three adjuncts: "other than the triad of adjuncts."
One should ascertain—that is, know—the Self as the witness of that; this is the meaning.
(14) Through association with the five sheaths and so forth, it remains as if identical with each of them.

The pure Self, like a crystal through its association with blue cloth and so forth. (15) Now, one might object: "Since the Self exists pervading the sheaths (kośas), such as that consisting of food (annamaya), and remains identified with each of them, how can it be eternally liberated? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Through the five sheaths, etc. The five sheaths are those consisting of food, vital breath, mind, consciousness, and bliss. By the word "etc.," eating and other such functions are included. Through association with these—that is, through a false identification—the Self appears as if it were identical with them; yet it is pure, for it is not in reality characterized by attachment to them.

Indeed, this person consisting of the essence of food (*annarasamaya*) and so forth indicates Brahman as residing within the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) solely for the purpose of perceiving subtle reality, but not from the perspective of ultimate truth (*tattvadṛṣṭi*). The meaning is that just as a pure crystal appears to be composed of various colors through association with blue, yellow, or other cloths, yet in reality there is no coloring, so it is here.
Furthermore, [the self] is joined with sheaths (*kośa*) such as the physical body, husk, and so on; when these are threshed by means of reasoning, [the inner core remains].
One should discern the inner, pure Self, just as one [discerns] rice from its husk.

(16) He describes the method of discerning through the knowledge of the nature of the unattached Self: "The body... etc. The body is the gross physical frame; like that, it is like the husk. Just as rice is covered by husks and the like, so too does the inner Self remain enveloped by the five sheaths (*pañcakośa*). Through the striking of reasoning—that is, by means of threshing in the form of logical inquiry—one should discern the pure [Self]; the meaning is that one should know it through discrimination.
16–17. Although the Self is always omnipresent, it does not manifest everywhere;
it manifests only in the intellect (buddhi), like a reflection in clear surfaces.

Now, one might ask: "If the Self is indeed all-pervading, why then is it not seen everywhere by everyone? To this he replies: "Always all-pervading. Although the Self is all-pervading and remains pervading everything, it is not manifested by the dull senses whose functions are directed outward; rather, it is manifested only when the intellect (*buddhi*) is unpierced by attachment and other afflictions, but not everywhere. The meaning is that just as a reflection is seen only in clear surfaces such as mirrors and not elsewhere, so it is in this case. (17)
One should always know the Self as distinct from the body, senses, mind, intellect, and primordial nature (prakṛti), and as the witness of their activities, like a king.
(18) By means of the illustration of the king’s man, he describes the indifference of the Self even while residing within bodies: "The body, senses... and so forth.

Of what nature are the body, senses, mind, intellect, and primordial matter? They are insentient (*jaḍa*), subject to transformation (*pariṇāmin*), and objects of perception (*dṛśya*). One should know the Self as distinct from these—the body, senses, mind, intellect, and primordial matter—which are insentient, perceptible, and subject to change; it stands as the witness (*sākṣin*) of their functions. Just as a king, remaining in his own city while his ministers are active, stays observing them as a witness, in that very same way one should understand [the Self].

To those lacking discrimination, the Self appears as if active when the senses are engaged, just as the moon appears to be running when the clouds are rushing along. (19) Now, one might object that it is illogical for the Self to be changeless, since it is seen to be always active; to this, he replies: "When the senses are engaged," and so forth.

While the senses and other faculties are active, the Self appears as if it were active to those who lack discrimination—those devoid of the instruction of teachers and scriptures—but not so to those who perceive reality.

Just as when fragments of clouds move due to the force of the wind, the moon also appears to the people as if it were moving, yet the moon itself does not move; such is the meaning regarding the Self as well.

Relying upon the consciousness of the Self, the body, senses, mind, and intellect function toward their respective objects, just as people rely upon the light of the sun. [Objection: But surely the body, senses, mind, and intellect are themselves perceived as conscious; what need is there for a Self? To this, he replies: "relying upon the consciousness of the Self. (Verse 20)

Depending upon the self-consciousness whose nature is eternal knowledge, the body, senses, mind, intellect, and so forth, function with respect to their own objects and respective domains; just as living beings carry out their activities by depending on the light of the sun, therefore consciousness belongs to the self alone, while the body, senses, and so forth are indeed insentient—this is the meaning.
The body, the senses, the qualities, and actions are superimposed through lack of discrimination upon the stainless *saccidātman*, just as blueness and other attributes are superimposed upon the sky.

(21) Now, one might ask: "How can the Self be changeless, given that it is incessantly experienced in such ways as 'I am born,' 'I experience the stages of childhood, youth, and so forth'? To this, he says: "The body, the senses... and so on.

The attributes of the body, senses, mind, and intellect, as well as the qualities of the three *guṇas*—sattva and the rest—and the actions consisting of the functions of the organs of action, though falsely identified with it, reside only in the stainless, unattached Supreme Self, whose nature is existence, consciousness, and bliss; because of their proximity to this Self, they appear [as its attributes] through non-discrimination, just as blueness and other qualities appear in the sky.
Therefore, these are not the attributes of the Self, but belong only to the body and so forth; such is the meaning.

Due to ignorance, the limiting adjunct of the mind (mānasopādhi), agency and other such qualities are superimposed upon the Self, just as movement and other attributes are attributed to the moon reflected in water because of the water itself.

Anticipating the objection that agency, enjoyership, and so forth are unavoidable because they are constantly experienced by the Self, he states that even these are likewise false: "Due to ignorance," etc. (verse 22).

The meaning is this: due to ignorance, the attributes such as agency and so forth belonging to that very mental adjunct (*mānasopādhi*) are superimposed upon the Self by the power of non-realization of truth; just as the movement and other qualities of water are superimposed through lack of discrimination upon the moon reflected in the water, so it is here.
Attachment, desire, pleasure, pain, and so forth, proceed only when the intellect (*buddhi*) exists.
In deep sleep that [intellect] does not exist; upon its destruction, therefore, it is of the intellect and not of the Self.

The Vaiśeṣikas and others indeed consider desire, aversion, pleasure, pain, and so forth to belong to the Self; he refutes that: "attachment, desire, etc."—all such things as attachment, desire, pleasure, pain, and effort belong only to the intellect, and not to the Self.

How so? When the intellect (*buddhi*) is present during the waking and dreaming states, attachment and other such qualities arise; when that intellect is destroyed—dissolved into its cause during deep sleep—they do not arise. Therefore, the meaning is that these are attributes of the intellect alone, and not of the Self (*ātman*).
Just as light belongs to the sun, coolness to water, and heat to fire.
The intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the Self is existence, consciousness, bliss, eternity, and purity.
(24) Anticipating the question, "In that case, what is the nature of the Self?", the text teaches the nature of the Self: "Light.

Just as light alone is the nature of the sun, coolness of water, and heat of fire, so too existence, consciousness, bliss, eternity, and purity are the nature—the essential form—of the Self. This is the meaning.

24–25. By joining together the two— the aspect of existence and consciousness belonging to the Self and the modification of the intellect— through non-discrimination, one proceeds with the thought, "I know."

If the Self is unchangeable, then how is it that there is the cognition "I know"? In response to this inquiry, he says: "Of the Self"—that is, of the inner Self (pratyagātman)—there is the aspect of existence-consciousness (saccidaṃśa). Furthermore, there is the "reflection of the Self" (ātmābhāsa), which is like a part (aṃśa) [of the Self], and the modification of the intellect (buddhivṛtti). By joining these two together through non-discrimination—even though there is no conjunction whatsoever of the unattached Self with anything—it is possible for a blending to occur due to the power of ignorance. Thus, the cognition "I know," which is a modification of the ego (ahaṃkāra-vṛtti), proceeds; yet, the appearance remains that there is no modification at all in the pure inner Self.

The self has no modification, and there is never any cognition of the intellect; having realized that the individual soul is entirely impure, one is deluded by thinking "I am the knower" and "I am the seer. 26.
This very point is clarified: there is no modification (*vikriyā*) of the Self;
the Self is by its very nature devoid of modification. There is never even the slightest suspicion of cognition in the intellect (*buddhi*).

Nevertheless, the individual soul (*jīva*), which is the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) accompanied by the light [of consciousness]—that is, the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) accompanied by the light—having known everything, becomes deluded, meaning it falls into the error of thinking, "I am the knower," or "I am the seer."
Having perceived the self as the individual soul (jīva), like a snake in a rope, one should carry fear;
but if it is known that "I am not the jīva, I am the Supreme Self," then one becomes fearless. 27.
He says that the Self, through its own lack of discrimination, superimposes the attributes of another upon itself and thereby fears—just as in the case of a rope-snake.

Just as one might experience fear, trembling, and so forth by superimposing the nature of a snake onto a rope in dim light or similar conditions, so too the Self superimposes the state of being a living individual (jīvatva) upon itself; perceiving itself as having a second and as limited, it experiences fear and becomes submerged in an ocean of suffering.

When knowledge of the meaning of the scriptures has arisen through what is taught by the scriptures and the teacher, then, beholding one's own Self with the eye of discrimination as being of the singular nature of indivisible bliss and knowledge, and realizing from that "I am not the individual soul (jīva), I am the Supreme Self (paramātman)," one becomes happy, free from fear and suffering.
The One illumines the intellect and the other senses.

A lamp, like a jar or other objects, is not illuminated by those insentient things themselves. [Objection: But how is it that the Self is not perceived—that is, not known—by the intellect (*buddhi*), mind (*manas*), ego (*ahaṃkāra*), and so forth, which are in such extreme proximity? To this he replies: "The Self" (verse 28). Although the Self exists in its absolute solitude, it illuminates the intellect, mind, ego, and so forth; yet the Self is not illuminated by those insentient things such as the mind. The meaning is: just as a single lamp illuminates all things such as jars, yet the lamp is not illuminated by those jars and the like, so it is in this case.
28–29. Because the Self is of the nature of consciousness, there is no desire for excessive awakening regarding its own awareness; just as a lamp has no need for another lamp to illuminate itself.

If it is argued that the Self is not manifested by the intellect, ego, and so forth, and therefore there must be another cognition for the knowledge of the Self, he says in response: "In its own awareness.

Since the Self is of the nature of consciousness (*bodha*), when its own awareness is eternal, there is no dependence whatsoever on another cognition for the awareness of that Self, because it is of the nature of experience itself. The meaning is that just as a lamp has no need for another lamp at the time it illuminates itself, so it is here.

One should know the identity of the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman) through the great sentences (mahāvākya), after negating all limiting adjuncts (upādhi) by means of the scriptural statement "not this, not this" (neti neti).

[Verse 30] If the Self were not knowable through the intellect and other such faculties, then another means for the knowledge of the Self would have to be stated; he asks what that means is, and says: "by negating," etc.

Now, therefore, follows the instruction: "Not this, not this. By means of Vedic statements that negate what is not [the Self], one should negate all limiting adjuncts (upādhis) after knowing them to be non-self and thereby casting them aside. Through great sentences (mahāvākyas) such as "That thou art" and "This Self is Brahman," one should know—that is, attain—the knowledge of the identity of Brahman and the Self by way of indication (lakṣaṇā).
The meaning is that it is to be known in this manner.

The visible body and so forth are products of ignorance, perishable like bubbles; one should know that the stainless "I am Brahman" is distinct from these. Anticipating the objection—"What is lost if there is no removal of that which is not the Self (atattva) during the knowledge of the true nature of the Self?"—the author states "āvidyakam" (products of ignorance), with the underlying intention that without the removal of the non-Self, the Self cannot be known. Just as the knowledge of the rope does not arise unless the superimposed snake is removed by the thought "this is not a snake," likewise, the Self is not known as long as the non-Self has not been discarded. Thus he says: "āvidyakam."

One should know that the entire collection of objects of perception, such as the body and the senses, is born of ignorance because it is an object of perception; like bubbles, it is perishable and transitory. Contrary to this, I am indeed Brahman—stainless, free from limiting adjuncts, eternal, one, and consisting of existence, consciousness, and bliss. From that, one becomes one who has accomplished all that was to be done; this is the meaning. (31) Because I am distinct from the body, there is no birth for me, nor dullness, emaciation, dissolution, and so forth.
There is no attachment to objects such as sound, nor is there [attachment] due to being devoid of sense organs.

(32) Having thus known the Self as non-dual bliss through the direct realization of the meaning of the Great Sentence (*mahāvākya*) according to the method described, he explains the manner of contemplating the Self by means of the Self within the Self alone—supported by one's own experience—in five verses: "Because of being other than the body," etc.:

because of being other than the gross body whose nature consists of inertness, visibility, and so forth, "for me" (*me*), there is no birth, inertness, emaciation, and the like; and because of being unattached to the senses and so forth, there is simply no experience of attachment to the enjoyment of objects such as sound.
Because I am without a mind, I have no suffering, attachment, aversion, fear, and so forth;
for according to the teaching of the Śruti, "He is indeed without breath, without mind, and pure," and so on.
"Because it is without mind" (amanastvāt).
Having raised the doubt that this [Self] does not manifest through the senses, vital breaths, or mind, he cites scripture as proof: "Without breath" (aprāṇa); the meaning is clear.
"Devoid of qualities, devoid of activity, eternal, free from conceptual construction,
stainless, changeless, formless, eternally liberated, and pure— I am [thus].
(34) Through the grace of the Guru, he expresses this reality established by his own experience in these three verses beginning with "nirguṇa."

I am devoid of qualities due to the absence of the intellect; I am actionless due to the absence of the senses and so forth; I am eternal because I am not an object of perception; I am free from conceptualization due to the absence of thought-constructs; I am untainted due to being unattached; I am changeless due to being partless; I am eternally liberated due to the absence of bondage; I am stainless due to being free from ignorance and its effects.
(34) I am like space, having entered all things, both within and without, and I am the infallible one.

"Always equal toward all, pure, unattached, stainless, and immovable. (35) Now, it has been stated that knowledge, characterized by the aforementioned reasons, is established as having such a nature; yet, one might ask, "What specifically is its nature? Anticipating this, he says: "I am like the ether. Like the ether, I am present within and without all that is visible and insentient, being *acyuta*, which means devoid of falling away (*cyuti*). Always equal toward all, I remain pervading everything with equanimity even amidst the uneven. Likewise, I am pure and untainted, and immovable because there is no movement for that which is full.
That which is eternally pure, liberated, one, indivisible, imperishable bliss,
truth, knowledge, and infinite— that supreme Brahman, I am indeed that.

"Ever-pure" means that which is one, indivisible bliss, non-dual due to the absence of a second, and is truth, knowledge, and infinite—that which is established by the Śruti as the Supreme Brahman; it is said that His very nature is "I am that very Supreme Brahman. 36.
In this way, the latent impression (*vāsanā*) "I am indeed Brahman," when cultivated without interruption, removes the distractions of ignorance just as an elixir (*rasāyana*) cures diseases.

[The author] states what human goal is accomplished by the reflection mentioned in the preceding verse when it has been practiced for a long time: "In this way, cultivated without interruption... and so forth.

In the manner thus described, the contemplation—"I am indeed Brahman"—when practiced continuously for a long time, destroys without remainder the distractions created by ignorance; the meaning is that it is just as a medicinal elixir (*rasāyana*), when used for a long time, destroys diseases without remainder.
(37) Sitting in a secluded place, free from passion, and having conquered the senses—
One whose mind is focused on nothing else should meditate upon that one Self, which is infinite.

(38) Regarding the rules for the means of contemplating Brahman, he says: "In a secluded place" means seated comfortably in a location free from contact with people; "dispassionate" means one whose desire has departed from everything, and therefore one by whom the senses have been conquered; "infinite" means the one, non-dual, undivided Self; and "one whose intellect is not otherwise" means one whose determinative intellect is established in Brahman alone—such a person should meditate, that is, contemplate.
Having dissolved the entire visible world into the Self alone by means of the intellect, the wise person should always contemplate the one Self as being like the stainless sky. 38–39.
To the question, "While the phenomenal world of the visible remains manifest, how can this contemplation of reality (tattvabhāvanā) be possible?", he says: "In the Self alone...

The wise one, possessing a purified internal organ, having dissolved—meaning having thoroughly destroyed—all that collection of visible objects within the Self alone during the time of meditative absorption (samādhi) by means of a pure intellect, should then contemplate and abide as the One Self, which, due to the absence of a second, is like the luminous space.
Abandoning everything such as form and color, the knower of the ultimate reality remains in the nature of perfect consciousness and bliss.

(40) The sage who perceives the ultimate reality, having abandoned all things such as name, form, and color, remains as the very embodiment of perfect knowledge and bliss; therefore, he says "form, color, and so forth," the meaning of which is clear.
In the Supreme Self, the distinction between the knower, the knowledge, and the object of knowledge does not exist; for,
being of the singular nature of consciousness-bliss, it shines by itself alone.

One might object: "Since the cognition of the triad beginning with the knower (the mother) is perceived as present, how can there be the contemplation of oneness? Anticipating this doubt, he states that there is no duality whatsoever in the Supreme Self: "The knower... (verse 41).
The imagined distinction between knower, knowledge, and the known appears within the Self; however, because its nature is one with knowledge and bliss, the Self shines and manifests by itself alone.

Thus, when the friction of meditation is constantly performed upon the fire-drill of the Self, the flame of arisen realization shall burn away the fuel of all ignorance. (42) Thus he states the perceptible fruit for one who meditates on the pure reality: "Thus the Self," etc.

The self alone is the lower fire-drill (*araṇi*), and the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is the upper fire-drill. When the churning of these two is performed constantly through meditation, the realization in the form of a flame that arises therein is knowledge (*jñāna*), which is wisdom (*vidyā*). This [wisdom] utterly destroys ignorance—the very fuel of primal ignorance—along with all its adjuncts. Then the seeker of liberation, consecrated in self-sovereignty, becomes one who has accomplished his purpose (*kṛtakṛtya*); this is the meaning. (42) Just as the previous dense darkness is removed by the dawn of awakening, so too is ignorance dispelled.
Then the Self manifests by itself, like the sun.

(43) When the dense darkness fashioned by ignorance has completely vanished through the knowledge of the absolute identity between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme (*para*), the Supreme Self manifests by itself; thus he says: "Like the sun...
Just as the sun manifests when darkness first perishes due to the light of dawn, so too does the Self. This is the meaning.
The Self, though eternally attained, appears as unattained due to ignorance; upon the destruction of that [ignorance], it shines as attained, like a necklace already around one's own neck.

Anticipating the student's thought—"Since the Self is by nature always beyond perception, it has never been attained; when, then, will that Self be attained?"—the author says: "But the Self is eternal," and so forth. The meaning is this: the Self is everywhere full, consisting of non-dual bliss, and is indeed always attained; yet, due to ignorance (*avidyā*), it appears as if unattained through delusion. Upon its destruction—that is, upon the destruction of the ignorance that veils it—through hearing the Great Saying (*mahāvākya*), it appears as if attained, according to the analogy of gold already present in one's own throat.

Just as the notion of a person in a post is produced through delusion, so too the notion of a living being (jīva) regarding Brahman—which is the true nature of the living being—ceases once that [true nature] is perceived. Now, one might object: "The identity of the living being with the Supreme Self is untenable, because the Supreme Self possesses a nature that is opposed to being a living being. To this, he says: "In a post... and so forth.

Just as people, when a post stands in the darkness, fear it might be a man due to the suspicion that it is a thief, so too, through a lack of inquiry, the state of being a *jīva* (individual soul) is superimposed upon Brahman. Likewise, when the true nature of that *jīva*—the referent of the terms *tat* and *tvam*—is seen and known through the vision of discrimination born from the instruction of the scriptures, the state of being a *jīva* also ceases, because it was merely imagined through delusion regarding Brahman; the meaning is that one realizes, "I am indeed Brahman.
Knowledge arising from the direct experience of the nature of reality immediately [dispels ignorance].
"And the ignorance of 'I' and 'mine' is sublated [by knowledge], like a confusion of the directions and so forth.

(46) Anticipating the objection—"While the notion of 'I' and 'mine' remains active, how can there be the notion of 'not-I'?"—he states that even that [notion of 'I'] is likewise false: "By the realization of the true nature," meaning that the knowledge arising from the experience of the oneness of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) sublates the ignorance of "I" and "mine"; the phrase "like a confusion of the directions and so forth" means that this is seen through direct experience.
The yogi who possesses right discernment beholds with the eye of knowledge the entire universe as abiding within his own self alone, and the Self as both the One and all.

When the notions of "I" and "mine" have perished, the yogi, possessing perfect discernment, beholds the entire phenomenal expansion of the visible world as his own self through the eye of higher knowledge; thus it is said:
"perfectly"—he perceives the one Self as everything, and at that time, he becomes of that very nature. This is the intended meaning.

"This entire world is indeed the Self; nothing other than the Self exists. Just as one perceives jars and other objects as being essentially clay, so too one should perceive the whole universe as one's own Self. (48) Now, an objection is raised: "The Self cannot be everything, because this contradicts direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). How can one see all this, which appears as manifold, as non-different from the Self? To this, he says: "This entire world is indeed the Self," and so forth.

This entire world is indeed the Self alone, because it is an effect of the Self; therefore, nothing other than the Self exists. Just as the effects such as pots and bowls are not different from clay, so too one perceives—sees—all that is visible within one's own Self without distinction, according to the Vedic scripture: "Modification is a mere verbal handle, a name; 'clay' alone is the truth. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.4) 48

But the one liberated while living (jīvanmukta), knowing that [Self], should abandon the qualities of his former limiting adjuncts; he should partake in the nature of existence, consciousness, and so forth, like a worm in a bee-hive.
He states that such a state indeed is liberation while living: "But the one liberated while living... and so on.

One should abandon the body, mind, intellect, and so forth—these being prior limiting adjuncts (upādhi) imagined by beginningless ignorance—as well as the qualities such as *sattva* and the rest. At that very moment, one is said to be liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*). Because he possesses the attributes of existence, consciousness, bliss, and so on, that *jīvanmukta* directly partakes of and attains Brahman, just like the worm in the *bhramara* flower; this is the meaning.
Having crossed the ocean of delusion and having slain the demons of passion, hatred, and the like...

The yogi, endowed with peace and delighting in the Self, shines forth. (50) Regarding how one who knows the Truth, delighting in the Self, dwells in happiness, it is said: "Having crossed the ocean of delusion. Delusion itself is an ocean because it is boundless; having crossed it by means of the boat of knowledge—that is, having destroyed it completely—and having utterly destroyed those demons such as passion and hatred which are the obstacles to liberation, he becomes "endowed with peace," meaning possessed of tranquility, self-restraint, and so forth. "Delighting in the Self" means one for whom the pleasure-ground (*ārāma*) and play are within the Self alone; such a person "shines forth," consecrated by his own sovereignty and manifesting in splendor.

Another meaning is suggested: Śrī Rāma, having crossed the ocean and slain the Rākṣasas such as Rāvaṇa, shines resplendent accompanied by Sītā alone, who is Peace (Śānti), and he flourishes in Ayodhyā;
[likewise], having abandoned attachment to external, impermanent pleasures, one is blissful in the Self.
Like a lamp within a jar, it shines eternally within.

He states the characteristic of one liberated while living: "Having abandoned external impermanent [pleasures]" means having discarded attachment and delight—along with their latent impressions—for impermanent pleasure arising from the objects of the external senses; the reason for this is that he is satisfied by the bliss of the Self.
Like a lamp within a jar, it shines only within; the meaning is that the bliss of self-realization, being witnessed by oneself alone, is not known by others.
(51) Although situated within limiting adjuncts, the sage remains untainted by their qualities, like the sky.
One should remain as if deluded by everything and move about unattached like the wind.

(52) He states that one who is liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) should conduct himself in this manner until the exhaustion of his *ārabdha* karma, according to the method described above: "Even though situated in the limiting adjuncts.

Although the sage remains as a witness within the limiting adjuncts of the body and so forth, he is not smeared by their attributes, just like the sky; he should contemplate, "I have no taint of karma. Even though he is all-knowing, he should remain like a fool, like an ordinary person. Unattached in all circumstances to objects obtained by chance, he should move about like the wind.
Through the dissolution of limiting adjuncts (upādhi), the sage enters into Viṣṇu without distinction,
just as water merges into water, space into space, or fire into fire.

He describes *videhakaivalya* (bodiless liberation) as occurring when the limiting adjunct of the body has dissolved upon the exhaustion of *prārabdha-karma*: "Due to the dissolution of the adjunct" (*upādhivilayāt*).

When the two bodies that constitute the adjunct have dissolved through the exhaustion of *prārabdha-karma*, the sage—the yogi—should enter into Viṣṇu, the all-pervading Supreme Brahman, in such a way that he becomes indistinguishable from it.
The illustration for this absolute identity is "water into water," and so forth. 53.
One should ascertain that Brahman is that gain from which there is no other gain, that happiness from which there is no other happiness, and that knowledge from which there is no other knowledge.
(54) Because Brahman is the substratum of all, it is described by means of an incidental definition (*taṭasthalakṣaṇa*) in these two verses beginning with "that gain from which... and so forth.

One should know that as Brahman that [attainment] beyond which no other attainment exists, because all attainments are included within it—just as all minor pleasures are included within the bliss of Brahman; that happiness beyond which no other happiness exists, because it is unsurpassed happiness; and that knowledge beyond which no other knowledge exists, because it is the cause of liberation, being the direct realization of Brahman.
(54) Having seen which there is nothing else to be seen, and having become which there is no rebirth.

"One should ascertain that Brahman is that which, having known it, there remains nothing further to be known. (55) "Having seen that" means that after seeing it, there is no other object to be seen, because by that very [vision] the goal of human existence (*puruṣārtha*) is accomplished; "having become that" means that having attained oneness with it, there is no more rebirth and so forth; "having known that" means that having known its true nature, there is no other thing to be known—one should ascertain that this very thing is Brahman.
The meaning is that all else is a vain display of scholarship.
(55) It is full above, across, and below— the non-dual reality of being, consciousness, and bliss.
One should ascertain that which is undivided, eternal, and one—that is Brahman.
He says, "Transverse, above, and below, everywhere Brahman alone is full. The meaning of "transverse, above," and so forth, is clear.
One should ascertain that Brahman is that which is undivided, one, and imperishable bliss, indicated by the Vedāntas through the form of the exclusion of what it is not (*atadvyāvṛtti*).

He states that Brahman, which is undivided, one, and bliss, is to be known through the Vedāntas by means of the exclusion of what it is not—that is, by way of negating what it is not—saying: "through the form of the exclusion of what it is not"; the meaning is clear.
All beings, beginning with Brahmā, depend upon mere fragments of that bliss which is of the nature of indivisible bliss; thus, they all become blissful according to their respective degrees. 58–59.

[Objection: But are not even Brahmā and the others heard in scripture to be possessed of unsurpassed bliss? To this he says: "Akhaṇḍa... and so forth. Brahmā, Indra, and the others possess only limited bliss; Brahman, however, is unlimited bliss because its nature is that of indivisible bliss (*akhaṇḍānanda*). Those such as Brahmā and Indra become blissful by resorting to a mere fragment of the bliss of Him whose very nature is thus, according to the gradation of bliss. This is based on such scriptural passages as: "Of this very bliss, other beings live upon a mere portion. (58)
Therefore, every object associated with that [consciousness] is permeated by consciousness in worldly experience;

consequently, Brahman is all-pervasive, like ghee in everything, O Śrī. Now, one might object: "If it is said that the Self alone appears as the object of supreme love, then how is it that the phenomenal world of the body and so forth is also experienced as being dearer? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Therefore, every object associated with that... and so on.

Even the entire body and other non-self entities are indeed dearer when conjoined with that Self; even worldly activity is dearer only when associated with it. Therefore, the all-pervading Brahman is the infinite Beloved. Just as clarified butter pervades all milk, so too, although Brahman is not a material entity, it appears as if dear because it pervades everything.
Thus, it is established that the Self alone is the dearest.
One should ascertain that Brahman is free from debt, neither gross nor subtle, neither short nor long, unborn, undecaying, and devoid of form, qualities, color, or name. 60.

Now, raising the doubt as to in what manner the Self remains pervading everything, and since it cannot be described directly—given the Vedic scripture stating "neither atomic nor gross"—it is said that it shines in the form of pure existence: "neither atomic nor gross," the meaning of which is clear. (60) That by whose light the sun and other luminaries are illumined, but which is not illumined by those things to be illumined;
One should ascertain that Brahman is that by which all this shines.

Furthermore, for the sake of knowing that Brahman, he explains it separately in three verses: "That which makes shine" (yadbhāsa)—that reality which causes the sun and other luminaries to shine, and which is not itself illumined by those objects of light such as the sun; for the Śruti says: "The sun does not shine there, nor the moon and the stars, nor do these lightnings shine, much less this fire; after Him, as He shines, everything shines; by His light all this is illumined. One should know that Brahman is that by which this entire world, consisting of the elements and elemental beings, shines.
61–62. Pervading both internally and externally by itself and illuminating the entire universe,
Brahman shines forth like a mass of iron heated by fire.
He says, "It shines forth as Brahman itself," meaning that like a red-hot iron ball, it pervades and illuminates everything both internally and externally; the meaning of "itself within" is clear.
(62) Brahman is distinct from the world, and there is nothing whatsoever other than Brahman.
If anything other than Brahman appears, it is false, like a mirage in the desert.

(63) He says this again: "That which is distinct from the world"—all that is indeed Brahman alone, which is real. Nevertheless, when one perceives it in the form of the world, it is not grasped as such; however, if it is investigated as the cause of the world through its distinction from the world, then Brahman can be known. Nothing exists apart from Brahman.
Whatever else is seen here, that is indeed false; the meaning is that it is like a mirage in the desert, like water superimposed upon the rays of the sun in a place devoid of water.
Whatever is seen or heard, if it is other than Brahman, that cannot truly exist.
And through the knowledge of reality, that Brahman is existence-consciousness-bliss (saccidānanda) and immutable.
Furthermore, he clearly defines that very Brahman with the words "it is seen":
through the knowledge of reality, all that is seen is Brahman—existence-consciousness-bliss, non-dual; the meaning is that there is nothing other than Brahman.
The eye of knowledge beholds the all-pervading Reality, which is Being-Consciousness-Bliss;
the eye of ignorance does not behold it, just as one with cataracts does not see the radiant sun.
And there is a Vedic revelation regarding heaven: "He is not grasped by the eye, nor by speech, nor by other deities, nor by austerity, nor by ritual action;
but when one's being is purified through the clarity of knowledge, then, meditating upon Him, one beholds Him who is partless."

If Brahman is all-pervading, then why is it not seen by everyone? Anticipating this doubt, the scripture establishes that it is not grasped by the eyes and other senses: "He who has the eye of ignorance does not see Brahman—though it is omnipresent, existent, conscious, and blissful—just as a blind man does not see the sun even though it is shining. The meaning is that through the clarity of knowledge, one sees Brahman alone everywhere with the eye of knowledge.
"Heated by the fire of knowledge kindled through hearing and other means, the individual soul (jīva), freed from all impurities, shines forth by itself like gold.

(66) Thus, even for one who has attained realization according to the method described above, some degree of ignorance may still occur due to the force of latent impressions (vāsanā) if they lack further practice; therefore, he says "through hearing and so forth" to indicate that one should again engage in hearing and the rest in order to eliminate that [ignorance].

The *jīva*, which is the inner self (*pratyagātman*), is intensely illuminated—that is, its knowledge is made manifest—by means of hearing, reflection, and so forth upon the meaning thus described. By that [knowledge], which is like fire, it is "heated," meaning it is thoroughly and specifically purified.
Thus, freed from the impurity of ignorance, which is the root of all transmigratory existence, it shines forth perfectly by itself, just as gold shines when heated by fire.
The Self, risen in the space of the heart, is indeed the sun of consciousness that dispels darkness;
all-pervading and sustaining all, it shines and illumines everything.

(67) Thus, the individual soul (jīva), having been purified, becomes the Supreme Self (paramātman) when risen in the space of the heart. Dispelling the darkness of ignorance (ajñāna), like the sun in the illumination of all forms, he says: "risen in the space of the heart."
Self-realization alone is the sun; because it is the foundational support of all, it is all-pervading and the sustainer of all. The rest is clear.
(67) It is independent of direction, space, time, and so forth; it is omnipresent, the remover of cold and other afflictions, eternally blissful, and stainless.
Free from all activity, he resorts to the sacred ford of his own Self; he becomes all-knowing, omnipresent, and immortal.

(68) Thus ends the *Ātmabodha*, composed by the venerable Śaṅkara Bhagavatpāda, disciple of the venerable Govinda Bhagavatpūjyapāda, the wandering ascetic teacher of the supreme order. Now, one might raise the objection that even for one who possesses self-knowledge, an effort to visit sacred fords such as Prayāga must be undertaken in order to remove the evil karma that obstructs knowledge. Anticipating this, the author states—beginning with "direction, place, time, etc."—that for one who has bathed in the sacred ford of his own Self, there is nothing further to be done.

He who, being free from ritual action (*viniṣkriya*), is a supreme ascetic (*paramahaṃsa*) and resorts to the sacred ford of his own Self (*ātmatīrtha*), he—being the nature of the Supreme Self—is all-knowing, omniscient, and omnipresent; thus he becomes immortal and liberated. Of what nature is this sacred ford of one's own Self? It is "all-pervading" (*sarvagata*) because it does not depend on direction, place, time, and so forth; it is "the remover of cold and other dualities" (*śītādihṛt*) because it removes the suffering of the pairs of opposites such as cold and heat; and it is "eternal bliss" (*nityasukha*) because it brings about the joy of liberation (*mokṣānanda*). The opposite of this should be understood regarding other sacred fords. Therefore, the sense is that for one who has bathed in the sacred ford of the Self, nothing whatsoever remains [unfulfilled].
Thus ends the Ātmabodhatīkā.
